report:
**Conclusion:** *Possibly, but the evidence is limited and inconsistent—so “yes” is too confident.* Olive leaf extract may modestly lower blood pressure in some people with mild hypertension, but it is not established as a replacement for proven antihypertensive treatment.

**What supports it:** A double-blind randomized trial in people with stage-1 hypertension found that olive-leaf extract (500 mg twice daily) lowered systolic and diastolic pressure similarly to captopril (12.5–25 mg twice daily). This is encouraging, but it was an active-comparator study rather than a placebo-controlled confirmation, and its result should not be interpreted as proving the supplement is broadly equivalent to prescription treatment.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0944711310002709

**Why uncertainty remains:** Another randomized, double-blind crossover trial specifically tested phenolic-rich olive-leaf extract and blood pressure, illustrating that the clinical literature is still relatively small and has used different products, doses, populations, and blood-pressure measures. That heterogeneity makes a reliable overall effect size hard to infer from these results alone.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486627/

**Practical takeaway:** Do not stop or reduce prescribed blood-pressure medicine based on olive leaf extract. Because supplements can have drug interactions and variable composition, discuss it with a clinician or pharmacist—especially if you take blood-pressure or diabetes medicines. NCCIH notes that herb/supplement interactions and product-quality issues are legitimate safety concerns.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/herb-drug-interactions
